facts.statement: The name Ectenosaurus means "drawn-out lizard" because of its elongated muzzle.
facts.quote: The generic name means "drawn-out lizard", from Greek ectenes ("drawn-out") and Greek sauros ("lizard") referencing the elongated muzzle.

facts.statement: Ectenosaurus had a skull about 64.5 cm long and an estimated total length of 5 to 6 meters.
facts.quote: With the preserved skull about 64.5 cm long, Ectenosaurus is estimated to have reached 5 - 6 m in length.

facts.statement: Ectenosaurus is characterized by its prominent elongated jaws, similar to those of Plotosaurus and Pluridens.
facts.quote: The most prominent of these features is its elongated jaws, elongated in a similar vein to other mosasaurs with elongated jaws, such as Plotosaurus and Pluridens.

facts.statement: Ectenosaurus had significantly smaller scales measuring 2.7×2.0 mm compared to the 3.8×4.4 mm scales of the similar-sized Platecarpus.
facts.quote: The scales are considerably smaller in size (2.7×2.0 mm) than those found in the famed LACM 128319 specimen of Platecarpus (3.8×4.4 mm), despite the animals being of similar sizes.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence suggests Ectenosaurus moved with a rigid anterior torso propelled by a tail fin, rather than undulating its entire body like a snake.
facts.quote: This also suggests that this section of the body was quite rigid during locomotion, and that the main form of propulsion would have to have been done by the tail (likely possessing a tail fin like other mosasaur species), and that it could not move by undulating its entire body like snakes do, a previously popular view of mosasaur locomotion.

facts.statement: Stable isotope analysis shows Ectenosaurus was one of the few plioplatecarpines capable of living outside nearshore marine habitats.
facts.quote: Stable isotope analysis indicates that Ectenosaurus was one of the few plioplatecarpines that was not restricted to nearshore marine habitats.

facts.statement: The animal was originally described as Platecarpus clidastoides by John Campbell Merriam in 1894.
facts.quote: Ectenosaurus was originally described as a species of Platecarpus, P. clidastoides, in 1894 by John Campbell Merriam.

facts.statement: Dale A. Russell re-described the species as the new genus Ectenosaurus in his 1967 book Systematics and Morphology of American Mosasaurs.
facts.quote: In his Systematics and Morphology of American Mosasaurs (1967) he re-described the species as part of a new genus, Ectenosaurus.

facts.statement: In 2021, Willman, Konishi, and Caldwell designated specimen FHSM VP-401 as the neotype for E. clidastoides because the original type specimen was destroyed.
facts.quote: In 2021, Alexander Willman, Takuya Konishi, and Michael Caldwell designated FHSM VP-401 as the neotype of E. clidastoides, as a replacement for the type specimen.

facts.statement: Kiernan and Ebersole named two new species, E. tlemonectes and E. shannoni, in 2023.
facts.quote: In 2023, Caitlín R. Kiernan and Jun A. Ebersole named two new species of the genus: E. tlemonectes from the Niobrara of Kansas and E. shannoni from the Mooreville Chalk of Alabama.

facts.statement: Fossils of Ectenosaurus are found in the Santonian and Campanian stages of Kansas, Alabama, and Texas.
facts.quote: Ectenosaurus is known from the Santonian and Campanian of Kansas, Alabama, and Texas.

facts.statement: Ectenosaurus lived between 89.8 and 72.2 million years ago, from the Coniacian to the Campanian.
facts.quote: Time range: Coniacian to Campanian (89.8 to 72.2 million years ago)

facts.statement: Ectenosaurus is classified within the Plioplatecarpinae subfamily of mosasaurs.
facts.quote: It is classified as part of the Plioplatecarpinae subfamily alongside genera like Angolasaurus and Platecarpus.

facts.statement: Some scientific analyses suggest Ectenosaurus belongs to the mosasaurine group rather than the Plioplatecarpinae, showing close relations with Prognathodon.
facts.quote: Some analyses recover it as a mosasaurine however, sharing close relations with Prognathodon.
